disprove.gloss: To show by evidence or argument that a claim, theory, or story is false.

senses.head: Show something to be false
senses.body: The core sense, and nearly the only one. The object is a claim, theory, rumor, or alibi — you disprove a statement, not a person. The -n participle *disproven* is standard in front of a noun (*a disproven theory*), but the perfect tense in edited American prose is usually *has disproved*.
examples: One clean experiment can *disprove* a decade of theory.
The lab *disproved* the original finding in under a month.
Nobody *has disproved* her central claim yet.
By 1960 the idea *had been disproven* several times over.
A *disproven* hypothesis still teaches you something.

senses.head: disprove a negative — the argument phrase
senses.body: A fixed idiom about the burden of proof: *you can't disprove a negative* means the person making the claim has to support it, not the skeptic. Common in debate, law, and science writing.
examples: You can't *disprove* a negative, so the burden stays with the accuser.
He *disproves* every rumor about the company by simply showing up.

engrave.gloss: To cut letters or a design into a hard surface — and, figuratively, to fix something permanently in the mind.

senses.head: Cut letters or a design into a surface
senses.body: The everyday sense, used of metal, glass, stone, and jewelry. In modern American English the verb is simply regular: *engraved* serves as both past and participle, and ✗ *has engraven* is a nineteenth-century form nobody writes now.
examples: They *engrave* the winner's name on the cup every June.
The jeweler *engraved* our initials inside the ring.
She *has engraved* glass for thirty years.
He *engraves* by hand, without a machine.

senses.head: Make a printing plate; produce an engraving
senses.body: The printmaking and currency sense: cutting an image into a plate or block so it can be inked and printed. Mostly technical or historical now.
examples: Winslow Homer *engraved* wood blocks for the illustrated weeklies.
US currency is still *engraved* rather than photographed onto the plate.
The bank note *had been engraved* by hand in 1890.

senses.head: Fix permanently in the memory
senses.body: Figurative, usually passive and followed by *on* or *in*: *engraved on my memory*. The nineteenth-century form *engraven* survives only as an echo of *graven image* in older hymns and poetry.
examples: That afternoon is *engraved* on my memory.
Thirty years of practice *have engraved* the movement into her hands.
The rule *had been engraved* in every trainee's head by week two.
Nineteenth-century hymns speak of a name *engraven* on the heart.

gnaw.gloss: To bite at something over and over with small, wearing bites — literally, or in the sense of a worry that keeps working away at you.

senses.head: Bite at something repeatedly
senses.body: The literal sense, typical of rodents, dogs, and teething children. Often with *on* or *at* when no hole is made, and with a direct object when one is. The g is silent in every form, /nɔ/.
examples: Puppies *gnaw* on anything within reach.
Something *gnawed* a hole in the bottom of the bag.
Mice *have gnawed* through the insulation again.
The dog *gnaws* the same bone every evening.

senses.head: gnaw at — nag, torment
senses.ru: грызть, мучить, не давать покоя (о сомнении, тревоге)
senses.body: Figurative, with a worry, doubt, guilt, or unanswered question as the subject. Almost always with *at*, and the feeling is persistent rather than sharp.
examples: Doubt *had gnawed* at him all week.
The question *gnaws* at me every time I drive past that exit.
Guilt *gnawed* at her for years afterward.

senses.head: Wear away gradually
senses.body: Of water, wind, rust, or inflation eating slowly into something. Written rather than spoken register; *gnawn* is rare enough in American print that you should write *has gnawed*.
examples: The river *gnaws* a little more of the bank away each spring.
Rust *has gnawed* the bottom of both doors.
In older writing you will find a rope described as *gnawn* clear through.

grave.gloss: An old verb meaning to carve or cut into a hard surface, now alive almost only in its participle *graven*.

senses.head: Carve or cut into stone or metal
senses.body: Archaic. Not the noun *grave* ("burial place") or the adjective *grave* ("serious") — this is the old verb that [engrave](#engrave) replaced. For anything you write yourself, use *engrave* or *carve*.
examples: Older writers use *grave* where we would now say *engrave*.
The mason *graved* the family name across the lintel.
Those letters *had been graved* into the stone centuries earlier.
The printmaker *graves* the plate first and pulls a proof afterward.

senses.head: graven — carved; cut deep
senses.ru: изваянный, высеченный; врезавшийся (в память, в лицо)
senses.body: The participle is the only part of the verb still in circulation, and it works as an adjective: the *graven image* of the Ten Commandments, or lines *graven* in a face by hard years. Slightly biblical or literary in tone.
examples: The commandment against *graven* images is the second one.
Two hard years *have graven* deep lines in his face.
The motto was *graven* over the doorway in Latin.

hew.gloss: To cut or chop something hard with heavy blows — and, in the commonest American use, to stick closely to a line, a plan, or a principle.

senses.head: Chop or cut with heavy blows
senses.body: The literal sense, used of timber and stone worked with an ax, adze, or chisel. Here the participle is *hewn*, especially before a noun: *hewn beams*, *rough-hewn stone*.
examples: They still *hew* the timbers by hand at the restoration site.
He *hewed* the beam square with a broadax.
Masons *have hewn* stone on this hillside since the 1800s.
The cabin walls were *hewn* from a single stand of pine.

senses.head: hew to — stick closely to
senses.body: Figurative and by far the commoner sense in American writing — of a policy, a script, a party line, or a schedule. This sense takes *hewed* in the perfect, not *hewn*.
examples: The committee *has hewed* closely to the original plan.
The adaptation *hewed* to the novel almost line for line.
She *hews* to her schedule no matter who complains.

senses.head: hew out — make by cutting away
senses.body: Carving something usable out of raw material or wilderness — a path, a road, a farm, a career. Carries a flavor of hard, physical effort even when the object is abstract.
examples: He *hewed* a path through the brush with a machete.
Crews *have hewn* a road out of solid rock.
Settlers *hew* a farm out of the woods one acre at a time.
Each block *had been hewn* to roughly the same size.

senses.head: rough-hewn — unpolished
senses.body: A fixed compound adjective, used of surfaces left rough by the ax and, by extension, of a plain, unrefined manner or style. Only the participle appears in this use.
examples: The furniture is deliberately *rough-hewn*.
His manner was *rough-hewn* but never rude.

melt.gloss: To go from solid to liquid under heat, or to make something do that; by extension, to soften, fade out, or disappear.

senses.head: Turn from solid to liquid with heat
senses.body: The core sense, both transitive and intransitive. *Melt* is a regular verb today — *the snow has melted*, never ✗ *has molten*. *Molten* survives only as an adjective, only before a noun, and only for furnace-hot material.
examples: *Melt* the butter first, then whisk in the flour.
The ice *melted* before we got the cooler open.
All the snow *has melted* off the north slope.
By noon the road tar *had melted* into black ribbons.
The furnace holds forty tons of *molten* iron.

senses.head: Dissolve in the mouth or in liquid
senses.body: Used of food that goes soft without any obvious heat, and of sugar or salt disappearing into a hot liquid. The compliment *melts in your mouth* is fixed.
examples: These cookies *melt* in your mouth.
The sugar *had melted* into the hot cream before she stirred it.
The cheese *melted* down into the bread.

senses.head: Soften emotionally
senses.body: Of a person, a face, or a heart giving way to affection or pity. Intransitive, informal and warm in tone; the transitive use (*that melted him*) is common too.
examples: Her whole face *melts* when the dog comes in.
He *melted* the second she started crying.
That video *has melted* every parent who has seen it.

senses.head: melt away — disappear gradually
senses.body: Of a crowd, a lead, a fortune, or a fear that shrinks to nothing rather than ending at once.
examples: The crowd *melted away* as soon as the police arrived.
His lead in the polls *has melted away* since June.
Whatever nerve she had *melted away* at the microphone.

senses.head: melt down — reduce to liquid; lose control
senses.ru: переплавлять; расплавиться (об активной зоне); сорваться, устроить истерику
senses.body: Three uses of one phrasal verb: melting metal down for its material, a reactor core melting down, and — informally — a person falling apart emotionally.
examples: They *melted down* the old trophies for the silver.
Reactor cores *melt down* when the coolant fails.
The toddler *had melted down* twice before we reached the gate.

senses.head: melt into — blend imperceptibly
senses.body: Of someone slipping out of sight into a crowd or a background, or of one color, sound, or landscape shading into another with no clear edge.
examples: He *melted into* the crowd before anyone got a photograph.
The hills *melt into* haze by mid-afternoon.
The suspect *had melted into* the neighborhood by the time the units arrived.

mow.gloss: To cut down grass or standing grain — and, in *mow down*, to cut down people or things in numbers.

senses.head: Cut grass short
senses.body: The everyday American sense: a lawn, a field, a ball field, a ditch bank. Americans write *have mowed*; *have mown* reads as British, though *mown* survives here as an adjective — *freshly mown grass*.
examples: I *mow* the yard every other Saturday all summer.
He *mowed* around the flower beds without being asked.
The crew *has mowed* the ball field twice this week.
Nothing smells better than freshly *mown* hay.

senses.head: Cut a hay or grain crop
senses.body: The older farming sense, where the point is the harvest rather than a tidy lawn. The field, not the crop, can be the object: *mow the back forty*.
examples: They *mow* the back forty for hay in July.
Crews *mowed* the alfalfa twice last season.
By the time we arrived, someone *had mowed* the whole hillside.

senses.head: mow down — cut down in numbers
senses.body: Of gunfire, a vehicle, or a disease killing or knocking down many at once, and in sports of a pitcher or team dispatching opponents easily. The idiom is always *mowed down*, never ✗ *mown down*.
examples: The truck jumped the curb and *mowed down* a row of mailboxes.
Machine guns *had mowed down* the first two waves.
Their closer *mows down* the bottom of the order every night.

prove.gloss: To establish that something is true, or to turn out to be a certain way.

senses.head: Show something to be true
senses.body: The core sense: evidence or argument that settles a question. In the perfect tense American prose prefers *proved*; *proven* is the form that goes in front of a noun — *a proven method*, *proven reserves*. The past is always *proved*: ✗ *he proven it in court*.
examples: Numbers by themselves don't *prove* much.
The prosecution never *proved* he was in the building.
She *has proved* every one of her critics wrong.
They only hire people with a *proven* track record.

senses.head: Turn out to be
senses.body: A linking verb, followed by an adjective, a noun, or *to be* — the subject is not being demonstrated to anyone, it simply turns out a certain way. This sense has no passive: ✗ *it was proved longer*.
examples: The drive *proved* longer than the map suggested.
The drug *had proved* safe in two earlier trials.
That shortcut always *proves* to be slower.
Time *proves* most confident predictions wrong.

senses.head: prove oneself — show what one can do
senses.ru: проявить себя, показать, на что способен
senses.body: Reflexive, about earning a reputation rather than establishing a fact. Also *prove someone wrong*, which is the commonest fixed pattern built on this verb.
examples: Rookies have to *prove* themselves all over again in the playoffs.
She *has proved* herself in three different departments.
He *proved* his doubters wrong in a single season.

senses.head: Prove a theorem
senses.body: The mathematical and logical sense: deriving a result from axioms or premises. Here *proven* is common in both slots — *has proven*, *a proven result* — more so than in ordinary prose.
examples: You can *prove* it in two lines with induction.
Wiles *proved* Fermat's Last Theorem in the 1990s.
No one *has proved* the conjecture in either direction.

senses.head: Test, put to the test
senses.body: The original sense, now archaic on its own but preserved in *proving ground*, in the saying *the exception that proves the rule*, and in the legal *prove a will*.
examples: "The exception that *proves* the rule" uses the old sense, "tests."
The desert *proved* every part of the vehicle.
The estate *had been proved* in probate court that spring.

senses.head: Rise, ferment (of dough)
senses.body: Baking usage, chiefly British; American recipes normally say *let it rise* or, as a noun-derived verb, *proof the dough*.
examples: Let the dough *prove* in a warm spot for an hour.
The loaves *had proved* overnight in the cooler.

reprove.gloss: To tell someone, formally and usually gently, that they have done something wrong.

senses.head: Rebuke someone mildly
senses.body: Formal and slightly old-fashioned; in speech Americans say *scolded*, *called out*, or *chewed out*. The participle is *reproved* — the -n form *reproven* is essentially unused, so never write ✗ *has reproven*.
examples: A good editor can *reprove* you without discouraging you.
The judge *reproved* both attorneys for talking over each other.
She *has reproved* him for the same habit more than once.
He *had been reproved* in front of the whole department.

senses.head: Condemn a practice or behavior
senses.body: Here the object is conduct rather than a person, and the tone is public and moral. The participial adjective *reproving* — *a reproving look*, *a reproving tone* — belongs to this sense too.
examples: The bishop *reproved* the practice in a letter to every parish.
Her silence *reproves* more effectively than any lecture.
The editorial *has reproved* the whole industry for looking away.
He gave me a *reproving* look and went back to his notes.

rive.gloss: To split or tear something apart with violence — a verb you now meet almost only in its participle, *riven*.

senses.head: Split or tear apart violently
senses.body: Archaic and literary in American English; ordinary prose uses *split*, *tear*, or *crack*. Watch the vowel: base and past have the long /aɪ/ of *drive*, but the participle *riven* shortens to /ˈrɪvən/ and rhymes with *given*.
examples: Old accounts use *rive* where we would say *split* or *tear*.
Lightning *rived* the oak from crown to root.
Frost *has riven* the ledge into loose slabs.
Every winter *rives* another crack in the foundation.

senses.head: riven — torn apart by conflict
senses.body: The one fully current use, and it is participial: an institution *riven by* scandal, faction, or doubt. Written register, common in journalism.
examples: The congregation *had been riven* by the vote on the building fund.
A company *riven* by that kind of argument loses people fast.
The party *has been riven* over the same question for a decade.

rot.gloss: To decay, or to make something decay; also, of people and things, to be left neglected until they fall apart.

senses.head: Decay, go bad
senses.body: The core intransitive sense, used of wood, fruit, meat, and cloth. *Rotten* is an adjective, not a working participle: write *the boards have rotted*, never ✗ *the boards have rotten*.
examples: Untreated fence posts *rot* within a few years.
The apples *rotted* on the ground before anyone picked them.
The floor *had rotted* through in two places.
Nobody wants a *rotten* board in a brand-new deck.

senses.head: Cause something to decay
senses.body: The transitive twin of the first sense, with damp, water, sugar, or salt as the subject.
examples: Water *has rotted* the sill under the window.
Damp *rots* wood faster than sun does.
Standing water *rotted* the roots within a month.

senses.head: Be left to languish
senses.ru: гнить, чахнуть, пропадать (в тюрьме, без дела)
senses.body: Figurative, of a person shut away or a thing abandoned: *rot in jail*, *left to rot*. Carries anger or contempt, so it is not a neutral choice.
examples: He can *rot* in there for all I care.
Two hundred boats were left to *rot* along the pier.
The proposal *had rotted* in a filing cabinet for years.

senses.head: Decay morally or institutionally
senses.body: Of a system, a culture, or an organization losing its integrity from within. Usually paired with *from the inside* or *at the core*; the adjective is *rotten* (*rotten to the core*).
examples: The whole system *has rotted* from the inside.
Discipline *rotted* under the third owner.
Institutions *rot* quietly long before anyone notices.

saw.gloss: To cut something with a saw, or to move back and forth the way a saw does. Note that *saw* is also the past tense of *see* — a different verb entirely.

senses.head: Cut with a saw
senses.body: The literal sense. The -n participle is British: Americans write *has sawed* and *sawed-off*, where British English has *sawn* and *sawn-off*. Do not confuse this verb with the past of *see*: ✗ *I sawed a movie last night*.
examples: *Saw* the boards to length before you carry them upstairs.
He *sawed* the branch off flush with the trunk.
I *have sawed* through this whole stack twice already.
The mill *saws* two hundred logs a day.
British lumberyards advertise *sawn* timber; American ones say dimensional lumber.

senses.head: saw off — cut off; sawed-off
senses.body: A common phrasal use, and the source of the fixed adjective *sawed-off* — a shortened shotgun, and, jokingly, a very short person.
examples: They *sawed off* the legs to fit the table under the window.
Someone *had sawed off* the padlock overnight.
A *sawed-off* shotgun is illegal in most states.

senses.head: Move back and forth like a saw
senses.body: Of hacking at something with a dull blade, or — with *away at* — of playing a bowed instrument energetically and not very well.
examples: He *sawed* at the steak with a butter knife.
The fiddler *saws* away for three hours straight.
She *had sawed* at the rope until her hands blistered.

senses.head: saw logs — snore
senses.body: American slang, always in this fixed phrase and usually in the progressive.
examples: He was *sawing logs* on the couch by nine.
Dad *saws logs* loud enough to hear from the driveway.

sew.gloss: To join, make, or mend things with a needle and thread.

senses.head: Stitch cloth together
senses.body: The core sense, by hand or by machine. Both participles are standard in American English, with *sewn* the commoner in edited prose. Pronounced like *so* and like [sow](#sow) — /soʊ/, never ✗ /su/.
examples: She can *sew* a straight seam faster than a machine.
The costumes *had been sewn* by volunteers.
My grandmother *sews* every curtain in the house.

senses.head: Make a garment by sewing
senses.body: With the finished thing as the object rather than the cloth. Often contrasted with buying something ready-made.
examples: She *sewed* her own wedding dress.
I *have sewn* three of these jackets and the lining still puckers.
He *sews* costumes for the community theater.

senses.head: Attach or mend by stitching
senses.body: *Sew on* a button, *sew up* a tear, *sew* a patch over a hole. The repair sense, and the one most people use most often.
examples: He *sewed* the button back on during the meeting.
Can you *sew* up this tear before Friday?
Someone *has sewn* a patch over the hole in the elbow.

senses.head: Close a wound with stitches
senses.body: The medical use, normally *sew up* or *sew shut*. In clinical writing *suture* is the technical verb, but *sew* is what everyone says.
examples: The resident *sewed* the cut closed in about four minutes.
The gash *had been sewn* shut before I even felt it.

senses.head: sew up — settle, secure
senses.body: An idiom for making an outcome certain — a contract, an election, a division title. This one always takes *sewed up*, not ✗ *sewn up*, in American usage.
examples: By March they had the contract *sewed* up.
One more win *sews up* the division.
The defense *had sewed up* the case by Wednesday.

shape.gloss: To give something a form with your hands or by force, or to influence how something turns out.

senses.head: Give something a physical form
senses.body: Working clay, dough, metal, or land into a form. *Shape* is fully regular today; the old participle *shapen* survives in exactly one word, the adjective *misshapen*, and never write ✗ *has shapen*.
examples: Bakers *shape* the loaves by hand every morning.
The wind *shaped* the dunes into long parallel ridges.
He *shapes* the clay with his thumbs, not with tools.
The fruit was small and *misshapen*, but it tasted fine.

senses.head: Influence how something develops
senses.body: The commonest sense in writing: an experience, a law, or a person that determines the course of something. Frequently passive — *shaped by*.
examples: Two teachers *shape* most of what a kid believes about school.
That one summer *has shaped* every decision I've made since.
The policy *had been shaped* by a single lawsuit.

senses.head: shape up — improve, get in line
senses.ru: взяться за ум, исправиться; привести себя в форму
senses.body: Informal, of behavior or physical condition getting better. The warning *shape up or ship out* is fixed.
examples: He *shaped up* fast once the coach benched him.
You need to *shape up* or find another crew.
She *has shaped up* considerably since the review.

senses.head: shape up — develop, turn out
senses.body: A different meaning of the same phrasal verb: how a season, a plan, or a situation is heading. Nearly always progressive — *is shaping up to be*.
examples: This *is shaping up* to be the driest June on record.
The season *shaped up* better than anyone expected.

shave.gloss: To cut hair off the skin with a razor, or to take a thin layer or a small amount off something.

senses.head: Remove hair with a razor
senses.body: The everyday sense, transitive or with no object at all. Use *shaved* in the perfect: *he has shaved his head since college*. *Shaven* is an adjective and lives inside compounds — *clean-shaven*, *close-shaven*, *freshly shaven*.
examples: I *shave* every other morning at most.
He *shaved* his beard off the day after the season ended.
She *has shaved* her head every summer since high school.
The new manager was young, *clean-shaven*, and visibly nervous.

senses.head: Take a thin layer off something
senses.body: Carpentry and cooking: paring material away in thin slices with a plane, a knife, or a peeler.
examples: The carpenter *had shaved* an eighth of an inch off the door.
*Shave* the chocolate over the top with a peeler.
He *shaves* the reed until it plays cleanly.

senses.head: Reduce by a small amount
senses.body: Figurative, always with *off* or *from* and a small quantity: seconds, dollars, percentage points, weeks of a schedule.
examples: He *shaves* a few seconds off his time every week.
They *shaved* four dollars off the ticket price.
We *have shaved* two weeks off the schedule already.

senses.head: Graze, pass very close to
senses.body: Less common, and mostly journalistic: a vehicle or a ball passing so close that it barely touches. The related noun is *a close shave*.
examples: The bus *shaved* the curb taking the corner.
His shot *had shaved* the post and gone wide.

senses.head: shave points — fix a score
senses.ru: намеренно занижать счёт (в спорте, ради ставок)
senses.body: American sports-betting term: players deliberately keep the margin of victory under the point spread. Always in this fixed phrase.
examples: Two starters admitted they *shaved points* that season.
Investigators showed the team *had shaved* points in four games.

shew.gloss: An old spelling of *show*, pronounced the same way — /ʃoʊ/ — and meaning the same thing; you meet it in the King James Bible and in older books and legal forms.

senses.head: Archaic spelling of *show*
senses.body: Not a separate verb: it is [show](#show) in its old dress, and it was never pronounced ✗ /ʃu/ to rhyme with *few*. In anything you write yourself, use *show*.
examples: Older printings *shew* the word where a modern edition prints *show*.
The 1611 translators *shewed* a clear preference for this spelling.
Editors *have shewn* it that way in every reprint of the text.
The old ledger *shews* every payment in a clerk's careful hand.

senses.head: shew mercy, shew forth — grant, display
senses.body: Biblical fixed phrases, the context in which most readers actually meet the spelling. Purely liturgical or literary register now.
examples: That psalm asks the Lord to *shew* mercy.
The chronicler *shewed* forth the whole history of the kings.
The manuscript *had shewn* the same reading before the page was damaged.

show.gloss: To let someone see something — and from there to demonstrate, guide, teach, reveal, be visible, or turn up.

senses.head: Let someone see something
senses.body: The core sense, with two objects: *show me the photo*, *show the photo to me*. The past is *showed*, the participle is *shown*: ✗ *he has showed me the file* wants *has shown*, and ✗ *he shown me the file* wants *showed*.
examples: Let me *show* you where the fuse box is.
He *showed* his ID at the door and walked straight in.
She *has shown* me that same photograph four times.
Both witnesses were *shown* the same lineup.

senses.head: Demonstrate, be evidence of
senses.body: With data, research, a record, or a result as the subject. The standard verb of scientific and news writing: *the study shows that…*
examples: The data *shows* a steady drop since March.
The audit *showed* no missing funds.
Two later studies *have shown* the opposite.

senses.head: Guide, lead someone somewhere
senses.body: Always with a direction word: *show someone in, out, around, to their seat, up the stairs*.
examples: An usher will *show* you to your seat.
She *showed* us around the plant for an hour.
They *had shown* him out before he finished the sentence.

senses.head: Teach by demonstrating
senses.body: Usually *show someone how to* do something — teaching by doing it in front of them rather than explaining.
examples: *Show* me how you tie that knot.
He *showed* the whole crew the shortcut in five minutes.
Nobody *had shown* him how the machine worked.

senses.head: Reveal a feeling or quality
senses.body: Of a person letting an emotion appear, or of a body, a machine, or a patient showing signs of something. Often negative: *never shows any nerves*.
examples: He never *shows* frustration on the mound.
The patient *showed* no signs of infection.
She *has shown* nothing but patience with him.

senses.head: Be visible
senses.body: Intransitive, with no object — a stain, a repair, a seam, or a feeling that can be seen. Also of pregnancy: *she's starting to show*.
examples: The stain doesn't *show* under the rug.
His nerves *showed* the whole first period.
The patch has faded so much it barely *shows* now.

senses.head: Exhibit or screen
senses.body: Of a gallery hanging work, a theater running a film, or an artist having work exhibited. Frequently passive: *her work has been shown in three cities*.
examples: The museum is *showing* forty of her drawings.
They *showed* the film twice a night all summer.
Her work *has been shown* in three cities.

senses.head: show up — arrive, appear
senses.body: Informal but extremely common; also of a thing becoming detectable — *the crack showed up on the X-ray*.
examples: Half the team never *showed up*.
He *has shown up* late to every rehearsal.
Nobody *shows up* to those meetings anymore.

senses.head: show off — display to impress
senses.body: Intransitive of a person behaving boastfully, transitive of the thing being displayed. Mildly disapproving; the noun is *a show-off*.
examples: He *shows off* every time there's a camera.
She *showed off* the new car for a solid ten minutes.
They *have shown off* that kitchen to everyone who visits.

senses.head: show someone up — outdo, embarrass
senses.ru: утереть нос, выставить в невыгодном свете
senses.body: The object goes between the verb and *up*. Distinct from *show up* meaning "arrive" — here someone is made to look bad by comparison.
examples: The intern *showed up* three senior analysts at the whiteboard.
He hates being *shown up* in front of his kids.

sow.gloss: To scatter seed on ground so it will grow — and, figuratively, to plant an idea or a feeling that will grow later.

senses.head: Plant seed
senses.body: The core farming sense, with the seed or crop as the object. Rhymes with *go*, /soʊ/ — the noun *sow* meaning a female pig is a different word, /saʊ/. Both participles are standard, but *sown* is the usual American choice.
examples: We *sow* the cover crop right after the last harvest.
He *sowed* rye across the whole back field.
The wind *has sown* thistle along every fence line.
She *sows* the small plots by hand.

senses.head: Plant a field with a crop
senses.body: The same action seen from the other end: the ground is the object, and the crop follows with *in* or *with*.
examples: They *sowed* the north forty in clover.
A field *sown* in late October comes up thin.
The terraces *had been sown* with barley for centuries.

senses.head: Spread an idea or feeling
senses.body: Figurative, and almost always something unwelcome — doubt, discord, confusion, panic. *Sown* is nearly automatic here. The proverb *as you sow, so shall you reap* belongs to this sense.
examples: Doubt *had been sown* long before the vote.
Those rumors *sow* confusion on purpose.
The memo *sowed* panic in half the building.

senses.head: sow one's wild oats
senses.body: A fixed idiom about reckless behavior in youth, followed by settling down. Traditionally said of young men, and dated in tone.
examples: He *sowed* his wild oats and then settled down fast.
Everybody's entitled to *sow* a few wild oats.

strew.gloss: To scatter things loosely over a surface so that they lie spread around.

senses.head: Scatter things over a surface
senses.body: The active sense: sawdust on a floor, petals on an aisle, gravel on a walk. Unlike most of this group, *strew* keeps its -n participle firmly in American English; *strewed* is acceptable but uncommon.
examples: They *strew* sawdust on the floor before every show.
The storm *strewed* branches across both lanes of the highway.
Someone *has strewn* gravel all over the walkway.
She *strews* wildflower seed along the ditch every spring.

senses.head: be strewn with — lie covered in
senses.body: The passive is the commonest shape of this verb. The surface becomes the subject and the scattered things follow with *with*: *the floor was strewn with paper*.
examples: The room *had been strewn* with unopened mail for weeks.
Papers lay *strewn* across every surface in the office.
The shoulder of the road was *strewn* with glass.

senses.head: Figurative — dotted with, full of
senses.body: Of a text, a career, or a record marked all over with something — errors, references, abandoned projects. Written register.
examples: His career is *strewn* with abandoned projects.
Every draft he *strews* with footnotes nobody can follow.
The report *had been strewn* with numbers no one could source.

swell.gloss: To get bigger — by puffing up, expanding, rising in number, or growing louder.

senses.head: Puff up (of the body)
senses.body: Injury, infection, or an allergic reaction. This is the sense that takes *swollen*: *my ankle has swollen*, *a swollen lip*. The past is always *swelled* — ✗ *my ankle swollen overnight*.
examples: Bee stings *swell* more than they hurt.
His ankle *swelled* within minutes.
Her knee *has swollen* to twice its normal size.
He walked in with a *swollen* lip and would not say why.

senses.head: Grow in number or size
senses.body: Of a crowd, a budget, membership, or a population. Growth in quantity normally takes *swelled* rather than *swollen*.
examples: The crowd *swelled* after the second band came on.
Membership *swells* every January and drops off by March.
Enrollment *has swelled* by a third since 2019.

senses.head: Rise, run high (of water)
senses.body: Of a river or the sea rising above its normal level. The related noun *a swell* is the long rolling wave that follows a storm.
examples: The creek *had swollen* over the low bridge by dawn.
Every river in the county *swells* after a week like that.
The channel *swelled* with runoff for three days.

senses.head: Grow louder (of sound)
senses.body: Of music, applause, or noise building gradually. Common in writing about performance; the musical noun is *a swell*.
examples: The strings *swell* under the last line of dialogue.
The chorus *swelled* until it filled the room.
The noise *had swelled* into something you could feel.
Applause *has swelled* every night this week.

senses.head: Fill with emotion
senses.body: Of a chest or a heart filling with pride, love, or anger. The fixed *a swelled head* means conceit, and takes *swelled*, not *swollen*.
examples: His chest *swelled* when they read her name.
Pride *had swelled* in him all evening.
Two good reviews *have swelled* his head considerably.

senses.head: Expand from moisture
senses.body: Of wood, seeds, beans, or paper taking up water and growing. Everyday practical usage.
examples: Wooden doors *swell* in humid weather.
The beans *swelled* to twice their size overnight.
The frame *had swollen* shut after a week of rain.

wax.gloss: To grow larger or stronger — said of the moon, and of moods, fashions, and reputations — and, in the everyday sense, to apply wax to something.

senses.head: Grow bigger (of the moon)
senses.body: The lit face of the moon growing from new toward full. Its opposite is *wane*, and the pair is fixed: *waxed and waned*. The verb is regular — *the moon has waxed*, never ✗ *has waxen*.
examples: The moon *waxed* all week toward Friday's full.
A *waxing* crescent is easiest to see just after sunset.
The moon *has waxed* and waned twice since we started counting.

senses.head: Increase, grow stronger
senses.body: Of influence, enthusiasm, or interest. Formal and slightly literary; usually paired with *wane*, and rarely used alone in speech.
examples: His influence *has waxed* and waned twice in ten years.
Interest in the case *waxes* every time a new document surfaces.
Enthusiasm *had waxed* considerably by the second rehearsal.

senses.head: wax poetic, wax nostalgic — become
senses.body: A linking use surviving in a handful of fixed collocations — *wax poetic, lyrical, eloquent, nostalgic, philosophical* — and usually with a light touch of mockery. You cannot extend it freely: ✗ *he waxed angry*.
examples: Critics still *wax* nostalgic about the first two albums.
He *waxed* poetic about a sandwich for ten minutes.
She *has waxed* eloquent on this subject before.

senses.head: Polish or coat with wax
senses.body: The ordinary modern sense, unrelated in feel to the growing one but the same regular verb: cars, floors, skis, surfboards.
examples: I *wax* the car twice a year.
She *waxed* the floors before the open house.
They *have waxed* these boards every fall since 1970.

senses.head: Remove hair with wax
senses.body: Salon usage, transitive with the body part or the person as the object. The related noun is *a wax*.
examples: She *waxes* her own eyebrows.
The salon *waxed* both her arms in twenty minutes.
I *have* never *waxed* anything in my life.
She lay very still, her face *waxen* in the lamplight.

whipsaw.gloss: To hurt someone from two directions at once — and, literally, to cut with a long two-handled saw.

senses.head: Hit from two directions at once
senses.ru: бить с двух сторон, зажимать в тиски (обстоятельств)
senses.body: The living American sense, a staple of business and sports writing, and usually passive: costs rising while revenue falls, injuries on both lines. Built on [saw](#saw) and following it in everything, including the American preference for *whipsawed* over British-flavored *whipsawn*.
examples: Rising rates and falling rents *whipsawed* small landlords last year.
The team *had been whipsawed* by injuries on both lines.
A thin market *whipsaws* anyone who trades on momentum.

senses.head: Be caught by market reversals
senses.body: The specific trading sense: a price that reverses just after you act, so you lose on both the entry and the exit. Nearly always passive — *whipsawed by*.
examples: Traders *have been whipsawed* by three straight reversals.
The index *whipsawed* between gains and losses all afternoon.

senses.head: Cut with a two-handled saw
senses.body: The literal woodworking sense, worked by two people pulling in turn. Nearly obsolete outside historical and milling contexts.
examples: Two workers *whipsaw* a log from opposite ends of the blade.
They *had whipsawed* every timber in the barn by hand.
Old mill records describe the planks as *whipsawn* rather than milled.

writhe.gloss: To twist the body, usually from pain or acute embarrassment.

senses.head: Twist in pain
senses.body: The core sense. The w is silent and the *th* is the voiced /ð/ of *bathe*, not the /θ/ of *both*. American English uses *has writhed*; ✗ *has writhen* is archaic.
examples: Burn patients *writhe* even under sedation.
He *writhed* on the field for a full minute before the trainer reached him.
The patient *had writhed* all night before the medication took hold.

senses.head: Squirm from embarrassment
senses.body: Figurative, of acute social discomfort. Often *writhe with embarrassment* or *writhe through* something.
examples: He *writhes* visibly whenever anyone brings up the old commercial.
She *has writhed* through worse interviews than that one.
I *writhed* in my seat for the whole toast.

senses.head: Twist, coil (of a shape)
senses.body: Of snakes, smoke, vines, or roots moving or growing in twisting lines. The archaic *writhen* meaning "twisted" survives only in poetry; modern prose reaches for *twisted* or *gnarled*.
examples: Snakes *writhe* when you pin them behind the head.
Smoke *writhed* up from the pile all afternoon.
Old poems describe *writhen* roots gripping the bare rock.
